In the past few weeks, there have been a number of online discussions among groups working on formalizing aspects of quantum computing. (Thanks to @Maris Ozols for organizing these!). I'm pretty sure there are many others we haven't talked to.

I think it is high time that these efforts coordinate!

Indeed, it would be great if the community could agree on an "API for quantum computing", so that the various ongoing projects can build toward a common library.

With this message, I'd like to gauge the interest for such a project.

So, who is working on quantum computing in Lean? What are you all up to? Can you share your repositories?

Most importantly, though: Would you like to participate in technical discussions for a common framework?

@Alex Meiburg, @Joseph Tooby-Smith, would PhysLib be happy to host this?

To get the ball rolling, let me briefly present our own effort.

For the past weeks, @Paradoxy and I have been working on QCLib, a library for talking about quantum circuits.

Our goal is to lay a solid foundation, as opposed to formalizing a particular result. (Accordingly, there's 0% gen AI content in the repo so far!).

The lower levels of abstraction are now pretty mature. At the bottom of the hierarchy are the files PiOuterProduct.lean and UnitaryGroup/PiKronecker.lean for reasoning about vectors in and unitaries on indexed tensor products ⨂iCdi\bigotimes_i \mathbb{C}^{d_i}⨂i​Cdi​. That's in contrast to the Lean QuantumInfo repo, which, as far as I can tell, focuses on (iterated) binary tensor products.

Based on these files, we have obtained some higher-level results, such as the basic theory of the Pauli group and a circuit decomposition of the quantum Fourier transform. (These are not as polished yet).

At the higher level, there are many technical design decisions to be made. For example, we initially worked with continuous linear maps on abstract Hilbert spaces (some remnants are in ExperimentsAndDeadEnds). For reasons I'm happy to discuss, this didn't seem worth the effort. But even if one restricts to concrete finite-dimensional objects, the question of which properties (such as unitarity or normalization) should be bundled isn't straight-forward at all!

So I'd be very happy if there were a critical mass of people interested in discussing these trade-offs, with the goal of defining a broadly useful API for quantum circuits!
[Tagging @Frédéric Dupuis @Dominique Unruh @George Afentakis @Andrés Goens @Carli Bruinsma @Dmitry Grinko @Felix Huber @Shreyas Srinivas @William Hasley @Marcus Rossel @Tanner Duve ]

Physlib would definitely be very happy to host this! :) We do have the Pi product, but there's no essentially zero API around it, since we just haven't needed it yet. I certainly agree that it's the correct choice for circuits over iterated binary products.
(We do have one place where we use iterated binary products, in reference to resource theories, but that's kind of by necessity of the axioms unfortunately.)

Alex Meiburg said:

Physlib would definitely be very happy to host this! :)

Great, thanks! :-)

We do have the Pi product,

For vectors / matrices / unitaries? I couldn't find it. There's Physlib.Mathematics.PiTensorProduct, but this seems to be about the basis-free theory.

Hello everyone, and thank you David for starting this discussion.

For the past couple of weeks, I have been working on formalizing "abstract" quantum computing from it's syntax / categorical description. Everything is available on this repo : QuantSem (also 0% A.I)

For now, I have sufficient basis to be able to describe quantum computation, build circuits and have usual coercions of finite data in unitary vectors and matrices for computation over finite-dimensional spaces.
In the end, I hope this description also shows the effect of higher-level type theory. Perhaps this would be a convenient way to build a formal link between quantum computation and linear-logic-related topics? (the structure of Quantum computing reminds me of MALL, the lack of LEM also prevents me from extending results over C* to results over C, perhaps the homotopy groups are at play here too?)
However, It is for now quite painful to write everything by hand. Many effects are usually hidden away, such as (and especially) reparenthesing. In this general setting, associativity is not an equality, but an isomorphism, forcing the user to write them down formally when constructing circuits. (Or, as I should start trying soon, construct the strictification of a monoidal category, which to the best of my knowledge is not a part of mathlib yet)
I hope to be able to develop an intermediate language, sufficiently human-friendly to be usable by anyone, while being able to automatically build those pesky nontrivial operations in a step similar to compilation. This could be an opportunity for a verified quantum compiler! (although I probably won't have the time to interface with an already known language such as QASM)

I'd be happy to discuss about the design decisions with the community. In the end, I spend a lot of time thinking about design, and It would probably be beneficial to have both an understanding of how people like to think about quantum algorithms, and how people envision the field as a whole.
(For know, the repo is quite messy when it comes to naming conventions, and implementations. I'm dissatisfied by the fact that I often have to copy-paste general definitions to some specialization, as mathlib may be enclined to treat stuff differently).

Hope this helps!

Glad to contribute from my side. I don’t know how feasible this is, but I wish to have interoperability between definitions of quantum and classical complexity classes. Further I want to ask if we can keep the computational aspects distinct from the physical aspects of QC.

I am also glad to accept PRs and reviews for quantum algorithms and complexity classes in Algolean per our discussion at the meeting. We recently had a STOC workshop poster for it.

I'm not an expert in Quantum info, but I strongly support any push in this direction.

What I think is important here is that everyone has the same idea of what the long-term vision is. Thinking about the Lean eco-system of monolithic libraries; where do we see quantum computing sitting into that?
I'm aware of two suggestions in this area:

  1. Everything within Physlib, in a directory e.g. ./Physlib/QuantumComputing/.... or ./Physlib/QuantumInfo/....
  2. The physics foundations as part of Physlib (as above), but having another repository for the more 'application' side of things which is downstream of both Physlib and CSLib. (Would need to think carefully about the scope of each part here).

Am I missing anything here? Which one suits this community better?

i’m also very interested in exploring the link between linear logic and quantum computing, as they seem directly connected via monoidal categories. my main interest in this field rn is whether this can inform the design of quantum PL and compilers @William Hasley

@Tanner Duve That's great! Hopefully this approach can be a direct illustration of your interests! I initially imagined it could be a bridge for complexity-related results / being able to apply proof complexity results to quantum algorithms (although I have no idea if such results already exist)

@Shreyas Srinivas , @William Hasley , @Tanner Duve : I understand that your work is one level of abstraction higher than the "linear algebra" theory @Paradoxy and me have been implementing.

I think it might be helpful to select one concrete example that we could work out together, to see how these approaches fit. Do you agree? Maybe Deutsch-Josza or Grover (we have versions of those for an older version of our library, but could quickly port them). Would that make sense to you?

@Joseph Tooby-Smith : Thanks for the message. I agree that both approaches could make sense.

In any case, our repository contains many very elementary definitions and results (e.g. on indexed tensor products) that I think should be part PhysLib / QuantumInfo regardless of whether higher-level work goes into PhysLib or elsewhere. (I think that some parts could be suitable even for Mathlib -- but given the review timelines there, it probably makes sense to upstream them to PhysLib first).

Now, at the moment, I don't even have a very clear picture how the quantum part of the original PhysLib and the QuantumInfo part will fit together in the longer term. Is there already a concrete plan? Are people working on this? Is help wanted?

I'll take the next few days to look at your definitions in more detail and try to come up with a proposal of how our stuff could fit in.

David Gross said:

Alex Meiburg said:

We do have the Pi product,

For vectors / matrices / unitaries? I couldn't find it.

Yes, it's not very findable. The construction is called piProd, it's there for CPTP maps as well as mixed states. (These are derived from more general ones for matrices and linear maps of matrices.) I'm not very happy with the style of it myself, even though I wrote it. :)
I added QCLib, QuantSem, and Quantum4Lean to the list. This is crazy! Since I made the list a week ago there were 5 new repos announced!!

At the risk of https://xkcd.com/927/ too hard, several people have talked about a "QuantumLib" of some sort. Ideally something that ends up under leanprover-community so that it gets some sort of official stamp. It's clear that more and more people want quantum computing in Lean to exist.

Mathlib has really succeeded, in large part because the idea of _Mathlib or it didn't happen_: there is one canonical place for math to live and you know that if you don't put your work then it will bitrot.

I'd really hoped that by merging QuantumInfo with PhysLean to become Physlib, and putting that under leanprover-community, we could get the same energy going. Unfortunately it seems to have backfired somewhat: some physicists aren't happy with the (overly computational, quantum-computing-oriented) definitions in QuantumInfo, so they don't want to contribute there. Others, as I've come to realize, find that Physlib is "too physics-y" and accordingly, since they're doing (quantum) CS, that's no home for them; CSLib is the closest thing, but it doesn't have any quantum stuff either and is moving a bit slowly in this regard.

How would people feel about a QuantumLib that lives downstream of both Physlib and CSLib, that aims - roughly - to provide these different perspectives in a common place?

Of course many parts of the library wouldn't depend on Physlib, and many parts wouldn't depend on CSLib; we'll simply have them as dependencies so that /when needed/ they can be used. (Accordingly, we should be a bit stricter than a blank import Mathlib\nimport Physlib\nimport CSLib.) Some parts will probably be pure-Mathlib-mathy-math, where things relate to complexity classes it'll use CSLib, and where (for instance) they relate to simulating Hamiltonians, they could import Physlib and interact with that.
I'd hope we could bring most of the different existing projects into one place, here.

Alex Meiburg said:

Yes, it's not very findable. The construction is called piProd,

I see, thanks. We do have significantly more API for this construction -- so this should be a good match.

Most of what we've written is pretty canonical. The one somewhat opinionated decision was to introduce a notation type class for "⊗" (it's implemented for the "big operator" version, and being ported to the binary version as we speak). This way, we could get rid of all the notational variants that distinguish between the t.p. for vectors / matrices / unitaries / hermitians, etc.
@Alex Meiburg : Algolean already lives downstream of both physlib and CSLib. I am happy to have to put quantum algorithms into it so that it lives side by side with classical complexity stuff.
I think at least the computational parts of QC should live side by side with classical algorithms and complexity theory.

@Shreyas Srinivas How do you see the split here? The core quantum stuff going in Physlib and the computational parts in Algolean?

From the point of view of a physicist, I would want some of the core API about quantum mechanics (specific Hilbert spaces, tensor products, bras, kets, mixed states etc.) to go in Physlib, because of it's application and use outside of quantum computing. Although this just comes down to carefully defining the scope and would work for any of the desired systems I think.

Having stared at Mathlib for a year, and at PhysLib for a day, here's my impression:

I think that Mathlib derives its value from providing an extremely well thought-out foundation for expressing math. In contrast, I feel like PhysLib has a number of extremely impressive particular results (e.g. Quantum Stein's Lemma, obviously!!), but the foundation is not yet nearly as solid. Is that fair?

Not having been there until yesterday, I can only speculate about the reasons:

  1. Physics never went through its own Bourbaki period. Our structures, methods, and results are not nearly as well-organized as is the case for mathematics. Every textbook has a chapter on the "axioms of quantum mechanics", but no two textbooks agree on what they are. (It's pretty amazing that physics as a field still works as well as it does).
  2. The person power hasn't been there. One needs a critical mass of quite dedicated people to discuss / implement / test / refactor the material.
  3. Maybe every larger library has to go through an initial phase, where a few projects are worked out till the end, so that one learns which definitions work well. Once the first experience is in, one can then revisit the roots and see what can be improved.

Now, at the moment, I don't even have a very clear picture how the quantum part of the original PhysLib and the QuantumInfo part will fit together in the longer term. Is there already a concrete plan? Are people working on this? Is help wanted?

I would say we are still in the transition phase here (whether that gets completed or pivots is another question). The initial idea was to merge the ./QuantumInfo part in with the ./Physlib/QuantumMechanics part so that they all use the same set up and framing. I would say that we are getting the people power for the main part of ./Physlib, but I think ./QuantumInfo hasn't seen much development since merging (no doubt, in part due to the reason Alex mentioned above), so things are still pretty fragmented.

In my message that started this thread, I said that I was interested in working on a "common framework" for quantum computing: The "basic API", like the lower-level modules in Mathlib. (In contrast, at this time, I'm personally interested in higher-level work, like formalizing an entire complex algorithm, only to the extend that it informs what is needed at the bottom).

I think that there's plenty of low-level stuff left to be done that is general enough that it should really be part of PhysLib, but that is too specialized for Mathlib (e.g. ways to combine few-body unitaries to define global dynamics).

For the foundations (i.e. the stuff which I think we will likely need in Physlib one day independent of anything else), maybe one idea here is that:

We start to develop this in ./Physlib/QuantumMechanics, using the things in ./QuantumInfo as a foundation, but bringing in other ideas, so we get a foundation which we have a consensus on.
(We are thinking about changing the way review works in Physlib, and this could be used here to form a team of reviewers with an interest in this area.)
@Joseph Tooby-Smith : This sounds excellent to me! If you need helping hands, count me in.
Is there a channel for this discussion? I guess it should happen under #PhysLib rather than under #Quantum information

Having starred at Mathlib for a year, and at PhysLib for a day, here's my impression:

I think I agree with all of your points here.

David Gross said:

Is there a channel for this discussion? I guess it should happen under #PhysLib rather than under #Quantum information

I see let's keep it here, since there are definitely some non-physlib questions here too! At least for the moment.

I would quite like to find a foundation for quantum computing, and quantum information and quantum physics, that fits different needs. A few of the differences I've noted:

  • Some repositories bake in a reliance on qubits. I think generally any Fintype should be usable as a basis in general. In particular, Pauli groups and Clifford groups make sense over Fin n, too.
  • Choosing to restrict to finite-dimensional theory, or not.
  • Choosing to carry around a canonical basis, or not. (If yes: matrices. If no: linear maps.)
  • Emphasis on computability / computational efficiency or not.
  • Quotient types make a very nice notion of working with kets and bras "up to phase". Physicists would generally never use this, but I think this is a clean way to describe the actions of circuits, including measurement outcomes and so on. It's not in any physics textbook as far as I'm aware. Of course there are case where it's convenient also to talk about them with a phase. Or ... or you can just do everything about density matrices.

The last point isn't really a big obstacle, since probably many theorems have versions for several of them. But the first ones, you really need to agree on things ahead of time, and it's hard to make things work together when they're not synced up.

@Joseph Tooby-Smith Tanner recently added deutschjozsa to Algolean. I think it is a good illustration of how quantum computation can live downstream of physlib. We use cptp maps from QuantumInfo in Physlib and build circuit types on it. Then we use Free monads to compose them and mvcgen to prove properties about quantum algorithms.

@Alex Meiburg : Agreed on all points. Another non-trivial decision is which kind of information should be bundled. Like:

  • Unitarity? Initially, we played around with plain matrices. But implementing the Pauli group without a properly-behaved zpow instance was no fun, so we ended up following "Lean QuantumInfo" and went with unitaries.
  • Normalization? Your definition of "ket" includes normalization information. As you note in the module docstring, this comes with downsides. What's the right decision here?

(I'm going to talk about my work, as I do not have in mind what Shreyas and Tanner developped)
I do not think comparing on a concrete example represents our work respectively. The aim of my project is to be able to talk about the entirety of quantum computing in a single language, and being able to get the most expressivity and computational power from this language rather than specific (setting related) benefits.
As such, I tend to focus on optimizing representation such that mundane tasks are automated thanks to the language. For instance, circuit equivalence relying on the inductive structure of the circuit can be fully automated with a tactic, as these rely on exchange laws resulting from the construction rather than the fact that in some hilbert space, everything works out.
Conversely, this lets me quickly switch between contexts, whereas maybe your library becomes too restrictive, I do not think specific examples really represent the whole work in this context. I'd rather we all agree on the boundaries of the project before settling on a standard.

(oops, i'm not familiar with zulip, this is an answer to @David Gross 's request from earlier)

@Joseph Tooby-Smith : A technical question, if I may (I'm just reading through PhysLib).

What is the function of the one-field structure QuantumMechanics.FiniteHilbertSpace?

The docstring says that it's preferred over using EuclideanSpace directly, as it has its own API. But does it? Is there any instance that should apply to one but not the other?

Thanks for the clarification!

My reason for wanting a simple example is that I'm not a computer scientist, so I have a limited understanding of what "being able to talk about the entirety of quantum computing in a single language, and being able to get the most expressivity and computational power from this language" means in practice.

@Alex Meiburg I agree with the idea of answering those questions before stating the scope of the project, but rather than ruling whether we want something or not, if the purpose of the library is to serve the most people in the most area, shouldn't we rather make sure to include everything and rather ask to which extent do we wish to develop these directions?
For instance, rather than judging that we should only talk about finite dimension, shouldn't we still talk about the general setting, and only work on it's refinement over finite dimensional spaces? This would allow for anyone to be able to contribute to the library, especially if the aim is to develop something not supported yet. (essentially we decide to not dedicate a lot of time to the setting we do not especially care about at the moment)
(this is only an example, I do not mean to imply we should only work on finite dimensional results)

(and allow me to be annoying for a bit by adding another point which I may be one of the few person in the world to care about : Should we keep the library constructive, or is usual mathematical logic (axiom of choice, LEM) our best friend in this setting ?)

I understand, I will try to explain my vision, (I hope this will be clear, please let me know if it wasn't. I am not really good at transmitting my vision)
The question I am trying to answer is : What is a Quantum Algorithm.?
The quick and (mathematically) valid answer to which is "a unitary map between hilbert spaces, and maybe measurements / non-trivial effects"

Although true, one may find that this radically differs from how people conceive Quantum algorithms : The most prominent model for which (as far as I know) is the Quantum Circuit. How people conceive computation over a quantum circuit has more to do with how the circuit is constructed, rather than it's mathematical meaning : Just by seeing the circuit, you are able to infer that perhaps, since part A and part B don't interact, their mathematical properties should not rely on one another, and thus your theorems should perhaps always rely on this fact.

Maybe a relevant illustration would be actual human languages : What I'm trying to do is to conceive some language (grammar system, ect..) such that it is :

  1. Natural and easy to use (essentially in the end, having some drawing software to interface with)
  2. With a minimal description (sentence), being able to carry the most meaning

A concrete example of a design-related question is : What is the syntax of Control gates? The easy answer is a big unitary that is described by it's effect on a basis. This is true, but sadly kills all hope for optimization and auto-theorem proving thanks to the circuit's construction. However, at a high level, control is an easy operation : Just select a wire, and a bunch of other contiguous wires, and give a family of gates related to the space over which the wire lives. So essentially, I have to come up with some "compilation"-related shenanigans to turn a high-level construction down to the ugly world of unitary gates that are well assembled together.
I now must design what it means to "take a wire", "take a family of unitaries" (this one is easy), and "compile down to the mathematical world"

The final objective, of course, is to not rely on setting-specific results, hence the part talking about describing the entirety of quantum computing within a single language

It's a frequent source of spirited debate between CSy and mathy contributors over in the #**mathlib4> channel. If you're feeling bored on a rainy Saturday afternoon, go there, post an innocent question about Finite vs Fintype and grab some popcorn. :-)

(Also, Alex is right: That ship has sailed for anything building on Mathlib).

I'm also interested in formalising quantum information, but I don't have a separate repository, I've only focused my efforts on contributing to mathlib. My take on it is that most of the math that we use is not specific to quantum information at all (in fact, most of you have probably heard the quip that quantum information is "just linear algebra", which has quite a bit of truth to it!). When it comes to formalisation, it is especially important to pay attention to this: one of the main principles underlying mathlib is that we want results that are as general as possible to avoid duplicating code and to ensure compatibility between different areas of the library. So to me, it doesn't make sense to code a separate, less general version of complex Euclidean space, of tensor products, matrices, and so on; what we use in quantum information are just special cases of what's already in mathlib, and if we want more API or there are missing results, mathlib will usually be the natural home for them.

That being said, there are things that indeed would make more sense in a specialised library or that would be better suited for CSLib, like a DSL for specifying quantum algorithms (i.e. being able to write a quantum program using do notation), and here we would want this to play nice with its classical counterpart, so that we could make statements about e.g. running time in a similar way. I would certainly be interested in this (and unfortunately I haven't had time to get involved with this effort in CSLib about classical algorithms!).

I think if we include quantum algorithms, there will be no way around having a large amount of similar structures and almost-duplication. This is less the fault of the quantum aspect, but rather of the machine model aspect. Even in classical computer science, e.g. if you want to talk about algorithm runtime, there exist a multitude of different machine models (many variants of Turing machines, many variants of RAM machines, each with some justification), with different details. Run-of-the-mill CS just ignores those differences. Picking one arbitrarily is probably not good because then we would force everything to use the same model. (Mathlib has it better because the number of relevant variations of the same things are lower.)

Personally, I would expect most of the mathematical foundations to belong to mathlib,
then a relatively thin layer of quantum specific math in PhysLib
and then most of the quantum algorithm stuff in something like CSLib. (I.e., everything that depends on concrete machine models and whatnot.)

Maybe where I'd expect more of in a quantum information repo would be things like entropies, computational uncertainty relations, etc. I.e., mostly things that do not relate to a runtime and complexity model. Those also tend to be more canonical.

I think at least on the computational side, speaking about individual models and relations between them is central to how the field is structured. Writing all quantum computing in a universal language would erase all these differences.

@Frédéric Dupuis : We already write algorithms do notation in our repo and prove them correct with mvcgen.

Yes, I completely agree. I've noticed several repositories independently redefining foundational concepts like Pauli matrices and qubits. It really is time for the community to come together and consolidate these efforts into a generalized, shared library.

Building on what has been discussed, I think one crucial aspect that hasn't been emphasized as much yet is the accessibility and usability of this unified library. As we figure out the theoretical scope and dependencies (whether components live in Mathlib, Physlib, or a downstream QuantumLib), we should also ensure that the library remains easy to load and quick to build. If we want broad adoption, it needs to be engineered so that users can pull it in and start working without dealing with massive build overhead or friction.

@Frédéric Dupuis. Thanks for chiming in.

I mostly agree. Any structure used in QM that's in principle of interest to a general mathematical audience should be formalized at a Mathlib level of generality and quality, and eventually be upstreamed.

But I think there are good reasons for maintaining a separate physics repository:

  • Some structures really are specific to quantum. For example, the discrete Fourier transform belongs into Mathlib, but the fact that it factorizes into O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) two-body gates -- absolutely central to its use in quantum computing -- doesn't strike me as the kind of statement that Mathlib would like to have.

  • A separate repository could serve as a "staging ground", where APIs can be tested out and mature before being upstreamed. Example: @Paradoxy and me wrote a "PiKronecker" module. We followed the layout of Mathlib's Kronecker.lean, but so far only implemented API for the special case where you fold * over entries (rather than a general function f : γ → γ → γ). That's easy to implement later, but why wait for that being done, if the current version already works for QC?

  • I feel it's unhealthy to think of Mathlib as the "only repository that really counts". This will lead to maintainers being annoyed because they are swamped with PRs. And it will lead to contributors being annoyed due to long review times and perceived gatekeeping.

It then seems that "develop your theory in a specialized repository, but aim at Mathlib-level of generality wherever it makes sense, and upstream once it's ready and battle-tested" is the best approach.

I substantially disagree that how "complicated" a definition is, is the relevant criterion. If that were the case, then docs#NNReal would certainly not belong in Mathlib, or indeed docs#Matrix at all. (Matrix A B C is always longer than its definition, A → B → C) I think it's pretty defensible to say those are both even more trivial abbreviations than "matrix with M^dagger=M".

So what makes a definition worth including? If it's a type that is a natural input or output of functions; if it carries invariants with it bundled together that are preserved under operations; and/or if it has semantics associated to it that distinguish it from the underlying type. To give concrete examples from Mathlib:

  • NNReal is naturally consumed by several functions, and output by others. This largely occurs in measure theory, we also see it as the return type of nonnegative norms. Matrix is naturally consumed and output by operations like "matrix product" or "matrix exponential". (Those would odd if written in terms of bare functions.)
  • NNReal carries the invariant of "nonnegative" with it. This is preserved under addition, multiplication, inversion, and NNReal.instPowReal. Accordingly, it is also preserved under integration as well as many other operations. It also behaves nicely with things like log and exp (although those are actually done with ENNReal, which builds on NNReal).
  • NNReal carries its own semantics for truncating subtraction: NNReal.instSub. This is something we wouldn't want as a global instance for any {x : T // 0 <= x}.
  • Similarly, Matrix carries its own semantics for multiplication. A -> A -> R has a separate pi-type pointwise multiplication that we want to keep distinct.

Compare this with Hermitian matrices.

  • Lots of operations only make sense with Hermitian matrices as input, like the Hermitian matrix CFC. Currently these are handled with junk values of 0 for non-Hermitian inputs. Sure, you could do the same with (E)NNReal: we could define Metric.eball and ENNReal.log to accept EReal instead, returning junk 0 on negative inputs, but that would be uglier.
  • Being Hermitian is preserved under many operations, again, arithmetic and the CFC being one big example. An early version of the QuantumInfo repo tried to do with the IsHermitian predicate and it was, frankly, terrible: very large amounts of code were being duplicated, because you had to construct an expression as well as the proof that it was Hermitian. (There were ways to avoid it, but they were almost always less convenient). In the same way that it's convenient to be able to write x + 2 * ε⁻¹ for x and ε as NNReal and already have the proof that it's nonnegative. This was compounded by the fact that several Mathlib functions (of pure data) required proofs of being Hermitian, instead of junk values, which left proof terms in values which were harder for certain tactics to work with.
  • Hermitian matrices have important semantics that they respect which we don't want to apply to standard matrices. Hermitian matrices form a Jordan algebra with a distinguished multiplication which is distinct from matrix multiplication (which doesn't apply to Hermitian matrices). That is, there are natural instances to put on a Hermitian matrix type which we would not want to put on the Matrix type.
  • Similarly, the Loewner order on Hermitian matrices gives closed intervals which correspond topologically to closed balls, and so the order is compatible with the topology in several nice ways that is not true of general (non-Hermitian) operators or matrices under the same order. (This is analogous to how, in principle, all of real analysis could be done entirely with complex numbers which happen to be real; but the inequalities would be a terrible pain.)

In the end I can make this statement:

Look, I and my collaborators worked for quite a while without this type. We had lots of issues with using Matrix.IsHermitian, and when we asked more experienced Lean/Mathlib users for help, the response was generally, "yes, this aspect of how Mathlib is built is bad, tactics can't handle this well, it's a pain and I'm sorry". So we made a type that made all of our code much cleaner and our development was much smoother.

It made our lives much easier, and the code much more readable, I think that is already a strong operational statement that this actually does matter.

Quantum computing is concerned with "systems with a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with a distinguished basis". Exactly the class of systems where the relevant objects have a canonical representation in terms of matrices. Matrices are easy to reason about, so basing a formalization on matrices gives a clean theory without too much pain.

Take POVMs. A general quantum library should certainly treat POVMs, including those with infinitely many outcomes. Their additivity property is phrased in terms of the weak operator topology. The WOT is stated in Mathlib for operators on a Hilbert space (thanks Fred!), so I guess all ingredients are in place. Now, Physlib could phrase basis-dependent finite-dimensional quantum theory in terms of continuous linear maps on Euclidean ℂ n, or keep Lean QuantumInfo's Matrix-based approach.

Either choice will lead to some amount of boilerplate. The first when restating general constructions for the matrix-based formalism, as for POVMs. The second e.g. when lifting concrete quantum gates (like the Hadamard gate), that are commonly specified in terms of their matrix representation, to the abstract linear algebra world.

It's my gut feeling that in the long run, the linear maps-based formulation is preferable. Though there might be practical aspects that I'm missing (Mathlib does restate large parts of linear algebra for matrices).

I think long term the social side the solution has been known by Mathlib for a long time, and it is the same formula we follow at Physlib:

  1. Do things openly (no big private repos that suddenly become public - I think these historically never get merged with the community libraries). It also means that others don't feel ownership over the project.
  2. Do things in small PRs, which are easy to review and look at. And have a review mechanism in place - and actively engage in it.
  3. Don't be scared to refactor, and openly encourage it.
  4. Have a clear vision (as David pointed out there are many different versions here going around...).

I think the basic goal here is: Make sure everyone feels some ownership of the project, no matter what stage they join.

On the topic of what a vision looks like, let me give something precise (the point here is to start with something, not to say this is 100% correct):

  1. Quantum computing is split across two libraries Physlib and AlgoLean.
  2. Results related to quantum foundations by necessity go into Physlib, as many have other uses in physics.
  3. Results related to computing (e.g. semantics, circuits, algorithms, compilation) go into *AlgoLean.
  4. Any result of general mathematical use, where the physics context does not matter, goes into Mathlib.

For the next part, some context: Physlib has within it three directories:

  • ./Physlib: This is the main physlib library, and has a solid peer-review level of review process.
  • ./PhyslibAlpha: This is really the 'development' area for physlib, arxiv-level of review, large PRs welcome, rapid devleopment.
  • ./QuantumInfo: The core of this is Alex's Lean-QuantumInfo repo. The idea was to eventually merge this with ./Physlib.

  1. We move (in one go) ./QuantumInfo into ./PhyslibAlpha. Cleaning up the structure and allowing
    rapid developement of quantum computing in the development area of Physlib.

  2. Rapid development of the quantum foundations can then take place in ./PhyslibAlpha, potentially pooling other Quantum-info repos that exist within this scope (similar suggested above).

  3. At the same time, we start moving solid, and agreed on results from ./PhyslibAlpha into the core Physlib library ./Physlib.
  4. To facilate the review process we can expand the reviewer team of Physlib to
    contain more quantum computing people.

What do people think? What would they want to change (and more importanly why?)?

(Naturally this doesn't solve the open questions about what is the right way to formalise things, but hopefully sets a foundation of where/how that can be done. I put AlgoLean in the above, but understand others may have different opinions about this, if so I think it would be good to articulate why.)

Edit: Quick follow up here (after a chat with David): I don't think moving ./QuantumInfo into ./PhyslibAlpha is the right idea, instead it seems good to let ./QuantumInfo to develop alongside the creation of basic API for quantum in Physlib, seems nice.

Why should QuantumLib exist?

There are clearly a variety of people who want to do quantum computing stuff in Lean. It's a shame when various projects are all in different descriptions and settings. At the start of the year, I had the hope that Physlib could become a common ground for this, but I quickly realized that many people from the information theory or quantum algorithms directions didn't see Physlib as a "home" for them. QuantumLib can, thus, hopefully get the community buy-in to become the canonical place for this.

By starting this as the merging of several different projects, with a variety of authors from different areas, I have high hopes that this can reach that buy-in. The plan is also to try to get it moved into leanprover-community (and set up a website etc., get it indexed in some of the Lean search engines).

Scope

I still think it's good for QuantumLib to exist, for the reasons I've explained -- there's community demand for it. Hi Alex and all, great initiative!

Maybe you would also find https://github.com/LionSR/QICLean interesting, which was very hidden inside our tensor network theory formalization work in https://github.com/LionSR/TNLean/
This formalization followed https://mediatum.ub.tum.de/doc/1701036/document.pdf/ with permission from M. Wolf.

With all the jewels there, especially yours, we did not set out to create another quantum library.

We focused on tensor network theory, which happens to use a lot of quantum information concepts and mathematical quantum many-body physics. Wolf's lecture notes are the standard reference in our environment for the minimal math needed to do research in these topics, and we were lucky to have direct access to him given our geographic and academic proximity.

So this lib mainly covers entanglement theory, channel representations, Kadison-Schwarz theory, quantum Perron-Frobenius and spectral theory, GKSL semigroups. Very technical graduate level quantum channel theory and mathematical theories of complete and positive maps etc. The overlap with the libs you mentioned should be little.

Following all the discussions as well, it is not clear where the lines fall between physics, mathematics, and algorithms. As our codebase grew, mixing the tensor network part with channel theory and CP maps became too complex, and that forced us to split them.
I sometimes wonder myself whether certain niche results belong in a "standard" library at all, and if so, which one: a standard QI library, a standard QC library, or a physics library?

Also, whether a definition is good or correct sometimes only becomes clear once downstream theorems test it. Without that feedback it is hard to judge a library's choices. Many of our definitions have been tested against tensor network applications. While during the formalization process they have also been reviewed heavily against the notes
